title: Choose the pattern from the constraint
description: Select the requirement that cannot be relaxed. The active route shows the smallest coordination pattern that fits it; select a component to inspect its responsibility.

nodes.label: Product request
nodes.detail: A user action or business change supplies the real constraint. Start here instead of deciding that every domain noun needs its own deployable service.

nodes.label: Order boundary
nodes.detail: Owns order state, the order API, and its private persistence. A boundary becomes a service only when autonomy is worth the added coordination cost.

nodes.label: Synchronous contract
nodes.detail: Carries a bounded request when the caller must know the result before it can complete its own business decision. It needs a deadline and an honest failure response.

nodes.label: Transactional outbox
nodes.detail: Stores an event record in the same local transaction as the owning service state, so a later publisher can reliably communicate the committed fact.

nodes.label: Payment service
nodes.detail: Owns payment authorization and its records. It exposes a versioned API; no other service writes its tables or treats a timeout as approval.

nodes.label: Inventory service
nodes.detail: Owns stock reservation. It can process a durable order event later, deduplicate delivery, and report a pending or rejected reservation to the workflow owner.

scenarios.label: One team, one release
scenarios.summary: The same team changes orders, payments, and inventory together, and one database transaction is required for the current product. There is no independent scaling or availability need.
scenarios.result: Keep a modular monolith with internal module boundaries. Document ownership now, but do not pay for network calls, duplicated operations, and distributed recovery before a real autonomy constraint exists.

scenarios.label: Immediate approval
scenarios.summary: Checkout cannot claim success until a payment provider returns an authorization decision. The customer needs a bounded, truthful answer in the request path.
scenarios.result: Use a synchronous payment API with a deadline, idempotency key, and explicit timeout outcome. Keep payment data private to its owner; a direct database read would hide the contract and couple releases.

scenarios.label: Independent stock work
scenarios.summary: Inventory has its own scaling and release cadence, and a reservation may be pending after the order is accepted. The product can communicate that pending state honestly.
scenarios.result: Commit the order and its outbox event locally, then let inventory reserve stock asynchronously. Use idempotent consumption and a workflow state such as reservation pending instead of a synchronous chain that makes checkout depend on inventory availability.

scenarios.label: Multi-step workflow
scenarios.summary: Payment, inventory, and fulfillment are independent owners. A later rejection must lead to a defined business action such as cancellation, release, refund, or manual review.
scenarios.result: Use a saga with a named workflow owner. Orchestration is usually clearer when timeouts and compensations matter; choreography can fit simple reactions. Neither option replaces local ownership, durable events, or idempotent handlers.
